tone_statements.citation: Wang, Lu, Binghao Wang & Yao Lu. 2026. Tai Nuea. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 56, e21, 1-17 (Illustrations of the IPA). doi:10.1017/S0025100326101108. Open Access CC BY-NC-ND.
tone_statements.quote: Modern Dai dialects in most of the areas where Dai is spoken (e.g. Xishuangbanna (= Sipsongphanna) [...] and Dehong [...]) still retain these characteristics. [...] In the Jinping Black Dai dialect, in live syllables there are both long and short forms for a. But in dead (=stopped) syllables the distinction no longer exists. Thus Tone 7 has merged with Tone 9, and Tone 8 with Tone 10. [...] 3. The number before the apostrophe in the Dehong and Luchun forms indicates the modern tone, while that after the apostrophe shows the ancient tone.
tone_statements.locator: p. 175 opening paragraph; p. 177 section I.3; p. 181 note 3
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)

tone_statements.citation: 杨光远 Yang Guangyuan & 刘建琼 Liu Jianqiong. 2024. 原始台语*ʔb、*ʔd声母在德宏傣语的反映形式 [The reflexes of the Proto-Tai initials *ʔb and *ʔd in Dehong Dai]. 民族语文 Minzu Yuwen 2024(5): 19-28.
tone_statements.quote: In terms of tones, Harris (1975) reports only five phonemic tones in Zhēfàng, Nam Hkam, and Van Poong Tong, contrary to Robinson (1994) who reported six tones similar to Mueang Sing (Wharton 2017a), Möng Vo (Gedney 1976) and Mángshì (Luo 1999), albeit with different mergers in the tones of the checked syllables (D tones). ... The six tones are A1, A23, A4, B123, C123, and C4, where the tonal category of B4 is the same as A23 ... Harris’ (1975) three 5-tone dialects simply lack the contrast between C123 and C4.
tone_statements.locator: p.22, section 2.1 'The Sound System of Modern Tai Nüa', text around Table 5
tone_statements.summary: Historical phonology; segmental changes only. Gives modern Tai Nüa 6 tonal categories (5 in Harris's dialects; Mángshì 1-6 keyed to Gedney boxes) from earlier authors; no pitch values.

tone_statements.citation: Lu, Yao & Jiangping Kong. 2019. A categorical perceptual study on Mandarin tones by native Dai language speakers in Dehong Autonomous Prefecture. IOP Conference Series: Materials Science and Engineering 612(3): 032055 (ACMME 2019), 8 pp. doi:10.1088/1757-899X/612/3/032055. CC BY 3.0.
tone_statements.quote: Chamberlain's view is based only on the pattern of tonal development: A1-234, B123-4, C123-4, DL and DS 123-4. The pattern of tone split in column A and the phonetic characteristics of the six tones in the Tai dialect of Muong Vat are not similar to those of Black Tai. The tonal analysis, the acoustical measurements of tones and the reconstruction of Old Black Tai tonal system which were done by the author support very well the idea proposed by Chamberlain, as illustrated in Figure 1.
tone_statements.locator: p. 76, section 'Tai Dialect of Muong Vat', with Figure 1 tone boxes 'Muong Vat 1 (Ban Phat)' and 'Muong Vat 2 (Ban Coc Lac)'
tone_statements.summary: Six tones (Gedney boxes, Chao values), Tai of Muong Vat, Son La VN; values = Ban Phat; Ban Coc Lac: 35, 42, 32, 42, 21', 44, DL 22/32, DS 45/34. Taped by Vietnamese colleagues; author's acoustic check.

tone_statements.citation: Cai R.N. [probably 蔡荣男 Cai Rongnan]. 2006. Acoustical analysis on the tones of Dai dialect in Dehong [English rendering by the citing source; Chinese title not established]. 河池学院学报 Journal of Hechi University 26(6): 80-82 (as cited in Lu & Kong 2019, ref. [14] 'Cai R N. Acoustical Analysis on the Tones of Dai Dialect in Dehong Country [J]. Journal of He Chi University, 2006, 26(6):80-82').
tone_statements.quote: Tai Nuea has nine tones: six unchecked and three checked. Among the unchecked tones, there are two level tones: a mid-level tone (T33) and a high-level tone (T55). … Additionally, there are two falling tones: a mid-falling tone (T31) and a high-falling tone (T51). … There are also two rising tones, T24 and T35. … There are three checked tones in Tai Nuea. T23 is a rising tone, with the f0 contour moving from low to mid … T31 is a falling tone, with the f0 contour moving from mid to low … T55 is a high-level tone, aligned with the tonal pattern of the unchecked tone T55.
tone_statements.locator: p. 13, section 'Tones' (tone table with examples on p. 12; Figure 12 f0 contours)

tone_statements.quote: b 和 d 分别来源于 ʔb、ʔd，出现在单数调，属于阴声调，g 出现在双数调，属于阳声调。版纳方言 b、d 声母的词出现在双数调，与各点都不同源。
tone_statements.translation: b and d derive from ʔb and ʔd respectively and occur with the odd-numbered tones, i.e. the yin tone series, while g occurs with the even-numbered tones, the yang series. In the Banna dialect the words with b-, d- initials occur in even-numbered tones and are not cognate with [the forms at] the other points.
tone_statements.locator: p. 20, footnote text at page foot
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)

sources.note: Mangshi (Dehong dialect) speaker; sections: Consonants (17), Vowels (monophthongs, a/aː length, diphthongs, triphthongs with acoustic data), Tones (nine: T33 T35 T31 T51 T55 T24 unchecked; T23 T31 T55 checked; durations), Syllable structure (CV, CVV, CVVV, CVC, CVVC), transcribed North Wind and Sun passage with phrase-boundary marks. There is no prosody/stress/intonation section and the word 'stress' does not occur.

tone.says: Presupposes the Tai 10-category lexical tone system (tones 1-6 live, 7-10 dead syllables by vowel length); states Dehong and Xishuangbanna retain vowel length and final stops, whereas in Jinping Black Dai loss of length in dead syllables merged tone 7 with 9 and 8 with 10, and in Wuding tone-8 words changed final stops to a nasal; Dehong forms are cited with 'modern tone' vs 'ancient tone' numbers, i.e. some Dehong words have shifted tone category; no tone values or inventory count given for De…

sources.citation: Chantanaroj, Apiradee. 2007. A sociolinguistic survey of selected Tai Nua speech varieties. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. xvi+187 pp.
sources.note: Ch. 2 reviews Proto-Tai tone boxes and the Tai Nua tone system (after Gedney 1976, Robinson 1994); ch. 5 lexicostatistics over 22 varieties (Mangshi, Ruili, Yingjiang, Zhefang, Gengma, Menglian area, Jinggu, Tai Mau Nam Kham, Tai Lai of Myanmar..), stripping 'presyllables and other extra syllables' before cognate comparison; tone-split diagrams per variety. No statement on word stress; 'accent' is used only for regional accent differences.

sources.citation: Luo Yongxian. 1999. A dictionary of Dehong, Southwest China. Pacific Linguistics C-145. Canberra: ANU (xl+338 pp; CC BY-SA online edition via sealang/CRCL).
sources.note: Introduction §2.1 (pp. xiii-xiv) gives consonants, vowels, diphthongs and six open-syllable tones (24, 53, 11, 31, 43, 33) plus three checked tones for Mangshi Dehong; §2.2 consonant/vowel/tone alternations; §2.3 word formation and four-syllable expressions. No statement anywhere about word stress/accent (a full-text search for stress/accent: stress/accent/prominence hits are dictionary glosses only).

sources.note: Image-only scan; scanned pp. 281-292 (whole introduction + 'Phonological Inventory'). sources.note: Historical study of initials, not a tone description: argues PT *ʔb, *ʔd > b, d (13th c., Ahom evidence) > m, n (15th c., Baiyi glossary) > modern Dehong m-, l- (v- in Jinggu/Jinping/Hongjin); tone enters only as the conditioning register - words from *ʔb/*ʔd carry odd-numbered (阴 yin) tones in Dehong, whereas Banna b-, d- words sit in even (阳) tones; no tone inventory or values in the pages scanned (1-4); pp. 5-10 not scanned.
